rationale.conceptual: The paper uses an established but non-trivial method (plane-wave pseudopotential DFT with LDA) applied to a complex surface reconstruction. Implementing it requires careful understanding of surface slab geometry, pseudopotentials, k-point selection, and interpreting surface state bands. There is no novel algorithm, but the domain expertise and the number of interacting components (slab construction, DFT setup, band identification) make it a 3.
rationale.execution: The reproduction pipeline has several stages: generation of the slab atomic coordinates, installation and configuration of a DFT code (Quantum ESPRESSO), running a self-consistent field calculation with specific cutoffs and a single k-point, and a post-processing step to extract band energies and wavefunction projections. This involves multiple tools, file I/O, and data interpretation, fitting a 3 on the execution scale.

difficulty.reasoning: The task requires reproducing a specific DFT result for a large surface slab model using standard LDA and plane-wave pseudopotentials. While the methodology is established, the domain knowledge needed to correctly set up the slab geometry, choose appropriate pseudopotential/cutoff parameters, and interpret the electronic structure is non-trivial. The execution involves multiple steps: constructing atomic coordinates, running a plane-wave DFT code, and post-processing the output to identify surface states and wavefunction localization. The pipeline is of moderate complexity, with environment setup and a few processing stages.

compute_estimate.reasoning: The plane-wave DFT calculation uses very low kinetic energy cutoffs (~72 eV) and a single k-point on a slab of roughly 200–300 atoms. This is computationally light by modern standards and can be run on a single CPU core with a few GB of RAM. Input data consists only of a pseudopotential file and atomic coordinates (MB-scale).
